Computer Engineering (PhD)
Why Pursue a PhD in Computer Engineering
This program offers doctoral students advanced training in areas considered to form the foundation of Computer Engineering, such as Computer Architecture, VLSI Design and Engineering Programming. Program curriculum provides a balance of theoretical and research-based courses, which will prepare graduates for advanced careers in engineering, technology and research.
Daytime and evening courses are offered to provide working professionals with the flexibility to customize their educational experience through full-time or part-time enrollment.
Research Labs and Facilities
Utilizing UT San Antonio’s state-of-the-art labs and equipment, Computer Engineering graduate students are conducting innovative research and refining their technical skills.
Some of the research labs include:
Autonomous Control Engineering
Cloud Computing, Quantum Computing
Control, Computation and Cybernetic Lab
Low Power VLSI
Matrix: AI Consortium for Human Well-Being
Neuromorphic Artificial Intelligence Lab
Robotics Lab
Unmanned Systems Laboratory
Learn From Expert Faculty
From artificial intelligence and machine learning to robotics and automation, program faculty are conducting innovative research and making meaningful contributions to the field. Our experienced faculty members are dedicated to providing hands-on learning experiences that prepare graduate students for successful careers in academia, industry research, or leadership roles.
College of AI, Cyber and Computing
This program is part of the UT San Antonio College of AI, Cyber and Computing, which advances expertise in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, computing and data science to meet the needs of a rapidly evolving technology landscape. The college fosters interdisciplinary collaboration, applied research and engagement with industry partners to drive innovation and address real-world challenges.

Admission & Application Requirements
Applications are submitted through the UT San Antonio Graduate Application. Please upload all required documents (listed below) on your UT San Antonio Graduate Application. It is the applicant’s responsibility to ensure completion and submission of the application, a nonrefundable application fee, and all required supporting documents are on file with UT San Antonio by the appropriate application deadline.

3.0 (on a 4.0 scale) Departments may consider GPA of last 60 semester credit hours

Frequently Asked Questions
What does UT San Antonio’s PhD in Computer Engineering focus on?
Student pursuing the PhD program will work faculty members in the department in areas including:
AI Systems
Cybersecurity
Cloud Computing
VLSI
Internet of Things
Autonomous Systems
Modern Computer Architectures
Neuromorphic Computing
Quantum Computing
How long does it take to complete a Computer Engineering PhD?
A Computer Engineering PhD typically takes about 3 to 5 years to complete after a master’s degree, though the exact timeline varies significantly by student background and research progress.
What are the career options after earning a PhD in Computer Engineering?
A PhD in Computer Engineering opens doors to advanced technical, research and leadership careers that are typically unavailable—or much harder to reach—with only a bachelor’s or master’s degree. Graduates are valued for their ability to create new knowledge, design complex systems and lead high‑impact technical efforts.
Typical career paths include becoming a tenure-track faculty member in academia, industrial research & advanced technical roles such as a Research Scientist, and advanced roles in Government, Defense and National Labs.
Does the program include hands-on lab research?
Yes. The PhD in Computer Engineering at UT San Antonio is strongly hands‑on and research‑intensive, with laboratory work forming the core of the doctoral experience, not an optional add‑on.
Are assistantships available for this program?
Yes. Assistantships are available for the PhD in Computer Engineering at UT San Antonio, and they are the primary source of funding for most full‑time PhD students. These positions are competitive and tied closely to departmental and faculty needs. Students are typically supported through Graduate Research Assistantships or Graduate Teaching Assistantships for the duration of the program.
In the News
UT San Antonio to launch nation’s first open-access neuromorphic computing hub (February 16, 2026)
UT San Antonio is set to launch the nation’s first open‑access neuromorphic computing hub, positioning the university at the forefront of next‑generation, energy‑efficient artificial intelligence research. The initiative, known as THOR: The Neuromorphic Commons, is led by Dhireesha Kudithipudi, PhD, a UT San Antonio computer engineering professor and Robert F. McDermott Chair in Engineering, and founding director of the MATRIX AI Consortium for Human Well‑Being. Funded by the National Science Foundation, THOR will serve as the national hub for open, public access to large‑scale neuromorphic computing resources.
Neuromorphic computing mimics the structure and function of the human brain, allowing systems to process information using a fraction of the energy required by traditional computing architectures. Unlike conventional processors, neuromorphic systems are event‑based, activating only when new information is present, which significantly improves efficiency and sustainability. Through THOR, UT San Antonio will make these advanced technologies accessible to researchers and students nationwide, creating the largest full‑stack neuromorphic computing platform ever made openly available for experimentation and discovery.
Under Dr. Kudithipudi’s leadership, THOR brings together a national network of academic partners, scientists and community leaders to expand training, collaboration and real‑world application of neuromorphic systems. By democratizing access to cutting‑edge hardware that has historically been limited to elite industry labs, UT San Antonio is accelerating interdisciplinary research and shaping the future of sustainable AI.
Read the full article “UT San Antonio to launch nation’s first open-access neuromorphic computing hub” to learn how UT San Antonio faculty are leading a national effort to redefine how intelligent systems are built and studied.
Advancements in Artificial Intelligence: the AI chip that doesn’t forget (Sept 30, 2026)
Researchers at the MATRIX AI Consortium may have solved a significant roadblock in artificial intelligence learning with the development of a new accelerator chip: Genesis. Dhireesha Kudithipudi, PhD, a UT San Antonio professor of computer engineering, worked with her team to create the chip in answer to a phenomenon known as “catastrophic forgetting,” in which artificial intelligence lacks the ability to retain previous knowledge after learning knew information, causing it to forget what it had previously learned. Genesis was designed to mimic the human brain’s ability to retain information and learn new information at the same time throughout its lifetime. The chip is also designed to be energy efficient and usable in areas with no data center or little to no connection, allowing it to be used in technology like implanted medical devices and field-deployed drones, going years without needing to recharge or reset. This could mark a significant advancement in the use of artificial intelligence.
